highlights.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # Inception’s Mercury 3: 40x Bigger, 8x Faster [2026] ![Daniel Roth](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/droth.webp) [Daniel Roth](https://shattered.io/author/droth/) Updated Oct 20, 2026 · 16 min read Inception announced Mercury 3 on October 19, 2026, calling it the most capable diffusion-based [large language model](https://shattered.io/category/ai-machine-learning/) the company has shipped. The release matters beyond the usual AI launch-day noise because Inception builds dLLMs, a different architecture from the autoregressive transformers that power GPT-6, Claude, and Gemini. Inception says Mercury 3 generates text at more than 1,000 tokens per second, runs 4 to 8 times faster than rival speed-optimized models, and beats GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 “across a range of benchmarks,” according to the company’s official announcement. The model is live now through the [Inception API](https://www.inceptionlabs.ai/blog/introducing-mercury-our-general-chat-model), plus third-party routes via Baseten, OpenRouter, and Vercel. Pricing lands at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.35 per million output tokens, undercutting most frontier-tier chat models on a per-token basis. Inception also expanded the context window to 1 million tokens and says the new model is more than 40 times the size of Mercury 1, the company’s original diffusion chat model. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## What Inception Announced on October 19 Inception describes Mercury 3 as “the most capable diffusion-based LLM released to date,” a description the company attached directly to its launch post. That is a notable claim from a company that, for most of its existence, has been treated as a research curiosity sitting outside the mainstream chatbot race dominated by OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google. Mercury 3 is the third generation of Inception’s commercial diffusion model line, following the original Mercury chat model that introduced the company’s approach to a wider audience. The headline figures are speed and scale. Inception says the model now exceeds 1,000 tokens per second in generation throughput, a number that, if it holds up under independent testing, would put Mercury 3 well ahead of typical throughput for chat-tier models from the major labs. The company also says Mercury 3 runs 4 to 8 times faster than the speed-optimized models it benchmarks against, which it names specifically as GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5. None of those comparative benchmark numbers have been independently reproduced as of this writing. They come from Inception’s own announcement and marketing materials. That distinction matters for anyone deciding whether to route production traffic to the new model, and it is a theme that keeps surfacing throughout this story: fast, concrete numbers around speed and price, paired with benchmark claims that outside labs have not yet verified. ## Diffusion LLMs, Explained for Readers Coming From GPT-6 and Claude Most of the chatbots people use today, including the GPT-6 family and Anthropic’s Claude line, are autoregressive. They generate text one token at a time, left to right, with each new token conditioned on everything written before it. That approach is reliable and well understood, but it is inherently sequential: token 500 cannot be produced until token 499 exists. Diffusion LLMs, the category Inception builds, work differently. Instead of writing left to right, a diffusion model starts with a noisy, incomplete draft of the full response and refines it in parallel steps, the same general idea borrowed from image-generation diffusion models like Stable Diffusion, but applied to text. highlights.content: [Skip to content](#main) Monday, October 19, 2026 [Advertise with us](/advertise)[About us](/about) [General](/general) # Two AI Agents Trigger Management Gridlock at Shanghai Big Tech Firm By [Sarah Chen](/author/sarah-chen)[China](/markets/china "More retail news from China") 2 min read | In this article (4) In October 2026, enterprise deployments of autonomous artificial intelligence agents across corporate teams in Shanghai are stalling, creating operational delays rather than labor savings. Corporate workflows designed to remove administrative overhead are generating dispute protocols between automated systems. Staff overseeing software agents report that the tools duplicate bureaucratic bottlenecks instead of speeding up execution. Rather than dividing task lists independently, automated systems require manual supervisor intervention to settle ownership boundaries. ## Protocols Stall on Ownership Disputes Operational trials in Shanghai show that automated digital workers struggle when interfacing across organizational reporting lines. When Xiao Mengjie, an artificial intelligence product marketing manager at a Big Tech firm in Shanghai, assigned routine tasks to two internal agents, the programs failed to execute. Her agent and a counterpart assigned to her supervisor entered an automated dialogue over verification requirements. Both digital workers debated which system held final ownership of separate deliverables, freezing task progress. > “It became very formal and cumbersome,” Xiao said. “Agents can create communication overhead too.” The resulting impasse mirrored human interdepartmental friction. Corporate teams must now assign staff to monitor routine communication logs between software programs to keep automated workflows running. ## Supervising Autonomous Systems Corporate managers across Asia face growing technical friction as technology platforms integrate agentic commerce tools into daily operations. Chinese technology groups including Ant Group have pushed deeper into agent-based commercial operations across consumer platforms such as Alipay, testing automated transaction handling. Deploying software agents inside corporate teams alters the daily cost structure for enterprise software users. Instead of reducing headcount requirements, administrative staff spend hours auditing logs, setting permission rules, and breaking deadlocks between autonomous routines. The technical friction sits directly inside the delegation logic. Programmed agents lean toward defensive verification loops when assigned overlapping corporate responsibilities, multiplying server calls and delaying project handoffs. ## Operational Costs Replace Promised Savings Software providers marketed autonomous agents across Asia as plug-and-play digital workers capable of managing complex business administration. The reality across engineering, marketing, and commercial teams is an extra layer of system supervision. Companies investing in agentic workflows must balance the cost of model inference against actual time saved. highlights.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # AI Agents Breached 100+ Firms at $50 a Site [2026] ![Daniel Roth](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/droth.webp) [Daniel Roth](https://shattered.io/author/droth/) Updated Oct 19, 2026 · 19 min read A single Chinese-speaking hacker used autonomous AI agents to break into the websites of more than 100 companies, including farm equipment maker Deere, appliance brand SharkNinja, and engine manufacturer Cummins, according to a [Reuters exclusive published October 19, 2026](https://www.tradingview.com/news/reuters.com,2026:newsml_L6N46118G:0-how-one-hacker-used-ai-agents-and-a-few-thousand-dollars-to-break-into-scores-of-sites/). The report, written by Raphael Satter, describes a campaign that probed more than 1,200 sites across the United States, Canada, Australia, and Japan, largely without direct human involvement at each step. The total cost to the attacker: roughly $5,000 in AI token spend, or about $50 per successful breach. The story marks one of the clearest public examples yet of AI agent hacking moving from theory to large-scale practice. Instead of a human operator manually scanning targets and writing exploit code, the campaign reportedly let AI systems do nearly all of the work: probing for weaknesses, adapting when an attempt failed, and grinding away at a target for hours until something gave. That shift, from AI-assisted hacking to AI-run hacking, is what security researchers have been warning about for more than a year, and it is now showing up in a named, dated, sourced news report rather than a hypothetical. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. The named victims include Deere, SharkNinja, and Cummins, three large industrial and consumer-products firms with extensive e-commerce and customer-facing web infrastructure. The campaign reportedly began on September 25 and focused on e-commerce websites in the United States, Canada, Australia, and Japan. What makes the case notable is not the number of victims alone. Mass-scanning campaigns against e-commerce sites are common. What stands out is how little direct human effort the operation apparently required. Reuters reported that the hacker’s own instructions to the AI agents were written in fewer than 100 Chinese characters, yet those few lines of guidance were enough to set off a sustained, adaptive intrusion effort against well over a thousand targets. The AI agents, not the human, carried out the bulk of the reconnaissance, exploitation attempts, and persistence. Successful intrusions typically took around 23 hours of probing and testing per target, a detail that matters for how defenders should think about this threat. That is not a fast, automated smash-and-grab. It is closer to a patient, overnight siege that a human analyst would find tedious and expensive, but that an AI agent can simply keep running at near-zero marginal human cost. ## Inside the Campaign: How Cairn Became a Weapon Central to the story is Cairn, described in the reporting as an open-source AI problem-solving platform. Cairn was not built as a hacking tool; it is a general-purpose framework for letting AI agents work through complex, multi-step tasks with access to tools like a shell, a browser, and file systems. highlights.content: ![](https://www.techtarget.com/rms/onlineimages/ai_a377464305_searchsitetablet_520X173.jpg) Blue Planet Studio - stock.adobe # Tenstorrent raises $1.5B to challenge Nvidia in AI servers and chip IP ## AI chipmaker reaches $6.2B valuation as it expands server production and licenses processor IP, but it remains to be seen whether it can offer a viable Nvidia alternative. ![Shane Snider](https://cdn.ttgtmedia.com/rms/onlineimages/snider_shane.jpg) Tenstorrent has raised $1.5 billion at a $6.2 billion post-money valuation, giving the AI chipmaker fresh capital to scale production of its Galaxy servers and expand its processor licensing business as it competes for workloads dominated by Nvidia. [The Series E round](https://tenstorrent.com/newsroom/tenstorrent-announces-series-e), which Tenstorrent said Monday it had closed, was led by Trace Capital and Innovation X, with participation from Fidelity Management & Research Company, T. Rowe Price, SanDisk, ARK Invest, Morgan Stanley and existing investors. Tenstorrent plans to use the funding to expand Galaxy server manufacturing and commercial deployments, develop new generations of its AI and RISC-V CPU intellectual property, and hire globally. The company did not disclose how it would allocate the capital among those priorities or provide a revenue forecast. For enterprise IT buyers, the central question is whether Tenstorrent can turn its alternative AI architecture into a dependable source of production compute. The company has named several commercial deployments and partners but has not disclosed revenue or a comprehensive breakdown of system shipments. Virtu Financial has deployed Galaxy servers on-premises for AI agents supporting trading and operations. Equinix offers Galaxy systems through its Distributed AI Hub, while [Smallest.ai](https://tenstorrent.com/newsroom/tenstorrent-and-smallestai-partner-to-bring-production-grade-voice-ai-on-prem) runs its Lightning V2 real time text-to-speech model on Galaxy Blackhole servers for organizations that want to operate voice AI on-premises. In Japan, ai& has deployed more than 120 Galaxy systems as part of its sovereign AI infrastructure, according to Tenstorrent. The new valuation is more than twice the roughly $2.7 billion implied post-money value of Tenstorrent's December 2024 financing, which raised more than $693 million at a $2 billion pre-money valuation. "The $6.2 billion post-money figure is ambitious but not crazy in today's AI infrastructure market," said Stephen Sopko, practice lead for semiconductor and deep tech at HyperFrame Research. "Think of it as paying a premium for a proven architect before the foundation is fully poured," Sopko said, pointing to CEO Jim Keller's track record and [investor appetite for alternatives](https://www.techtarget.com/it-infrastructure/news/366645030/Qualcomm-OpenAI-IBM-target-AI-infrastructure-efficiency) to Nvidia’s hardware and software stack. The valuation, he said, leaves room for execution risk because the company still needs to demonstrate that commercial deployments can scale predictably. ## Inference offers a path to compete Tenstorrent builds AI processors around its Tensix AI cores and develops [RISC-V](https://www.computerweekly.com/news/366541622/RISC-Q-rises-to-software-ecosystem-challenge) CPU technology. It sells compute systems ranging from individual cards and workstations to [Galaxy servers](https://www.techtarget.com/it-infrastructure/tip/10-top-AI-hardware-and-chip-making-companies-in-2026) and larger superclusters, while licensing its processor designs to companies developing their own silicon. The company is positioning its systems for inference -- running trained models to generate responses, code, images and video -- rather than trying to displace Nvidia across the entire AI market. The development marks a move to secure independent AI models and training technologies, shifting away from its previous strategy of relying on OpenAI models. The new model uses a mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture across all layers, with 2.8 trillion total parameters and 80 billion active parameters. MoE activates only selected expert networks depending on the input tokens. Its predecessor, MAI-Base-1, combined dense feed-forward networks with MoE layers. It had 1 trillion total parameters and 35 billion active parameters. MAI-Base-1 served as the foundation for MAI-Thinking-1, a reasoning model Microsoft unveiled in June. Microsoft said it trained MAI-Base-2 over 38 days in August and September using 16,000 Nvidia GB200 GPUs and a dataset containing 50 trillion tokens. The model is currently undergoing post-training to improve reasoning capabilities and safety. Microsoft is also preparing a next-generation reasoning model based on MAI-Base-2 while developing its successor, MAI-Base-3. Microsoft claimed that MAI-Base-2 outperformed other open-weight models tested against a separate evaluation dataset that was not used during training. In particular, the company said MAI-Base-2 achieved 4.2 to 12.3 times greater pretraining compute efficiency than China’s DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Base. It also reported a 6.3- to 12.7-fold improvement over MAI-Base-1. However, these figures do not mean that actual GPU processing speeds or inference costs improved by four to 12 times. Instead, they refer to the amount of pretraining floating-point operations (FLOPs) required to achieve equivalent evaluation performance. The results were derived using scaling laws that estimate the relationship between model performance and computational requirements by training models of different sizes. Microsoft also integrated vision capabilities from the pretraining stage. According to the company, vision-language data accounted for approximately 18% of the overall training dataset. This means the model was trained from the outset to understand both text and images. Microsoft said it improved computational efficiency by jointly designing the model and infrastructure and optimizing its data pipeline. The company also emphasized that it used proprietary training data whose sources it directly controlled, rather than distilling outputs from other AI models. The approach appears intended to demonstrate Microsoft’s ability to control the entire model development process independently. Meanwhile, Mustafa Suleyman, CEO of Microsoft AI, reportedly claimed during an internal meeting that MAI-Base-2 outperformed OpenAI models. Many people I speak to think of AI as a chatbot, like Microsoft Copilot, Claude or ChatGPT. You ask it a question, it answers, and you decide what to do with the answer. Agentic AI works differently, because it can act on your behalf. Take something as ordinary as booking a haircut. A search engine gives you a long list of local hairdressers to work through yourself. You could engage with a generative AI chatbot to narrow that down to a few suggestions that suit the style you want and what you're willing to pay. Either way, you still have to choose, call and book the appointment. An agentic system could do the rest. It could pick the best option against your preferences, contact the salon, agree a time, book and pay, and arrange your travel there. That change from giving answers to taking actions is what alters the risk, and the governance. ## Agentic AI vs AI agents The terms are often used interchangeably, but it helps to distinguish agentic AI from AI agents. Agents perform tasks autonomously or semi-autonomously within a constrained, task-specific scope, in response to prompts or human direction. Agentic AI operates with a high level of autonomy, completing multi-step tasks and working across systems and multiple AI agents towards a set goal. It’s also important to know that not all agents are created equal. There are different types – or tiers – of agents. They might differ in how independently they can operate, the permissions they have, their ability to interact with their environment, and the complexity of what they are being asked to do. You might have an AI assistant that can generate content, but it’s a bit like a chatbot and can’t take actions. The ‘pure’ definition of an agent is a software programme that can execute actions within its environment, subject to predefined constraints. Autonomous or multi-agent systems introduce a new level of risk. These can pursue goals with very significant independence and authority. **Peter Lee, partner and global head of AI governance, Simmons & Simmons.** ## How might agentic AI be used in legal services? As a solicitor, you could give an agent a goal, like creating a settlement proposal. The agent will break that goal down into steps. It might read the file, extract facts, identify issues and then compare them with similar matters. It might draft a note of advice before producing the proposal. Corporate workflows designed to remove administrative overhead are generating dispute protocols between automated systems. Staff overseeing software agents report that the tools duplicate bureaucratic bottlenecks instead of speeding up execution. Rather than dividing task lists independently, automated systems require manual supervisor intervention to settle ownership boundaries. ## Protocols Stall on Ownership Disputes Operational trials in Shanghai show that automated digital workers struggle when interfacing across organizational reporting lines. When Xiao Mengjie, an artificial intelligence product marketing manager at a Big Tech firm in Shanghai, assigned routine tasks to two internal agents, the programs failed to execute. Her agent and a counterpart assigned to her supervisor entered an automated dialogue over verification requirements. Both digital workers debated which system held final ownership of separate deliverables, freezing task progress. > “It became very formal and cumbersome,” Xiao said. “Agents can create communication overhead too.” The resulting impasse mirrored human interdepartmental friction. Corporate teams must now assign staff to monitor routine communication logs between software programs to keep automated workflows running. ## Supervising Autonomous Systems Corporate managers across Asia face growing technical friction as technology platforms integrate agentic commerce tools into daily operations. Chinese technology groups including Ant Group have pushed deeper into agent-based commercial operations across consumer platforms such as Alipay, testing automated transaction handling. Deploying software agents inside corporate teams alters the daily cost structure for enterprise software users. Instead of reducing headcount requirements, administrative staff spend hours auditing logs, setting permission rules, and breaking deadlocks between autonomous routines. The technical friction sits directly inside the delegation logic. Programmed agents lean toward defensive verification loops when assigned overlapping corporate responsibilities, multiplying server calls and delaying project handoffs. ## Operational Costs Replace Promised Savings Software providers marketed autonomous agents across Asia as plug-and-play digital workers capable of managing complex business administration. The reality across engineering, marketing, and commercial teams is an extra layer of system supervision. Companies investing in agentic workflows must balance the cost of model inference against actual time saved. When two autonomous programs stall over task governance, the enterprise pays for computing power while project timelines slip. Retail operators and technology platforms building agent-based customer services face similar risks. Unchecked automated negotiations between client-side bots and merchant systems can slow transaction completion rates and increase backend support tickets. ## Defining Boundaries for Digital Workers Technology groups spent much of late 2025 and 2026 rolling out generative software tools across commercial operations. Early rollouts focused on standalone generative tasks like copy drafting, which required little inter-agent communication. AI Agents.titleZh: AI Agent Hacking Spree Breaches 100+ Firms [2026]
AI Agents.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # AI Agents Breached 100+ Firms at $50 a Site [2026] ![Daniel Roth](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/droth.webp) [Daniel Roth](https://shattered.io/author/droth/) Updated Oct 19, 2026 · 19 min read A single Chinese-speaking hacker used autonomous AI agents to break into the websites of more than 100 companies, including farm equipment maker Deere, appliance brand SharkNinja, and engine manufacturer Cummins, according to a [Reuters exclusive published October 19, 2026](https://www.tradingview.com/news/reuters.com,2026:newsml_L6N46118G:0-how-one-hacker-used-ai-agents-and-a-few-thousand-dollars-to-break-into-scores-of-sites/). The report, written by Raphael Satter, describes a campaign that probed more than 1,200 sites across the United States, Canada, Australia, and Japan, largely without direct human involvement at each step. The total cost to the attacker: roughly $5,000 in AI token spend, or about $50 per successful breach. The story marks one of the clearest public examples yet of AI agent hacking moving from theory to large-scale practice. Instead of a human operator manually scanning targets and writing exploit code, the campaign reportedly let AI systems do nearly all of the work: probing for weaknesses, adapting when an attempt failed, and grinding away at a target for hours until something gave. That shift, from AI-assisted hacking to AI-run hacking, is what security researchers have been warning about for more than a year, and it is now showing up in a named, dated, sourced news report rather than a hypothetical. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## What Reuters Uncovered: The Core Facts According to the Reuters report, dated WASHINGTON, Oct. 19, a cybersecurity researcher spent the past couple of weeks watching a Chinese-speaking hacker break into websites belonging to more than 100 companies. The named victims include Deere, SharkNinja, and Cummins, three large industrial and consumer-products firms with extensive e-commerce and customer-facing web infrastructure. The campaign reportedly began on September 25 and focused on e-commerce websites in the United States, Canada, Australia, and Japan. What makes the case notable is not the number of victims alone. Mass-scanning campaigns against e-commerce sites are common. What stands out is how little direct human effort the operation apparently required. Reuters reported that the hacker’s own instructions to the AI agents were written in fewer than 100 Chinese characters, yet those few lines of guidance were enough to set off a sustained, adaptive intrusion effort against well over a thousand targets. The AI agents, not the human, carried out the bulk of the reconnaissance, exploitation attempts, and persistence. Successful intrusions typically took around 23 hours of probing and testing per target, a detail that matters for how defenders should think about this threat. That is not a fast, automated smash-and-grab. It is closer to a patient, overnight siege that a human analyst would find tedious and expensive, but that an AI agent can simply keep running at near-zero marginal human cost. ## Inside the Campaign: How Cairn Became a Weapon Central to the story is Cairn, described in the reporting as an open-source AI problem-solving platform. Cairn was not built as a hacking tool; it is a general-purpose framework for letting AI agents work through complex, multi-step tasks with access to tools like a shell, a browser, and file systems. That same flexibility is what made it adaptable to offensive security work once someone pointed it at a list of targets instead of a legitimate problem set. Many people I speak to think of AI as a chatbot, like Microsoft Copilot, Claude or ChatGPT. You ask it a question, it answers, and you decide what to do with the answer. Agentic AI works differently, because it can act on your behalf. Take something as ordinary as booking a haircut. A search engine gives you a long list of local hairdressers to work through yourself. You could engage with a generative AI chatbot to narrow that down to a few suggestions that suit the style you want and what you're willing to pay. Either way, you still have to choose, call and book the appointment. An agentic system could do the rest. It could pick the best option against your preferences, contact the salon, agree a time, book and pay, and arrange your travel there. That change from giving answers to taking actions is what alters the risk, and the governance. ## Agentic AI vs AI agents The terms are often used interchangeably, but it helps to distinguish agentic AI from AI agents. Agents perform tasks autonomously or semi-autonomously within a constrained, task-specific scope, in response to prompts or human direction. Agentic AI operates with a high level of autonomy, completing multi-step tasks and working across systems and multiple AI agents towards a set goal. It’s also important to know that not all agents are created equal. There are different types – or tiers – of agents. They might differ in how independently they can operate, the permissions they have, their ability to interact with their environment, and the complexity of what they are being asked to do. You might have an AI assistant that can generate content, but it’s a bit like a chatbot and can’t take actions. The ‘pure’ definition of an agent is a software programme that can execute actions within its environment, subject to predefined constraints. Autonomous or multi-agent systems introduce a new level of risk. These can pursue goals with very significant independence and authority. **Peter Lee, partner and global head of AI governance, Simmons & Simmons.** ## How might agentic AI be used in legal services? As a solicitor, you could give an agent a goal, like creating a settlement proposal. The agent will break that goal down into steps. It might read the file, extract facts, identify issues and then compare them with similar matters. It might draft a note of advice before producing the proposal. It runs a whole process, rather than providing a single response. ## The Law Society’s research on age...

Photo: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP As global governments and tech giants reckon with widespread of revelations of autonomous AI agents unexpectedly breaking into computer systems, documents obtained by The Intercept show the U.S. Army is looking to harness that exact technology to seek and destroy. Army Cyber Command is developing a platform to turn AI agents into autonomous weapons that can navigate and “neutralize” the computer systems of adversaries, the documents show. Since 2010, Army Cyber Command, or ARCYBER, has led the U.S. Army’s cyber operations. This includes the defensive effort of protecting domestic computer systems and the secretive offensive work of hacking military targets. So far, this has largely been the work of human soldiers operating computers, like those of the 780th Military Intelligence Brigade. But as the government races to adopt artificial intelligence technology, ARCYBER is looking to offload some of its attacks to AI. The nascent program, codenamed “ECHOTRIBBLE,” is based on one of the leading trends of the AI boom: agents. AI agents are essentially software programs that leverage machine learning technology, often large language models like Anthropic’s Claude, to autonomously accomplish tasks provided by their user. Consumers can deploy AI agents to schedule meetings, generate itineraries, make online purchases, or book tickets. Through ECHOTRIBBLE, the Pentagon plans to turn AI agents into tools of war “designed to autonomously navigate infrastructures” and capable of “identifying and neutralizing identified threats/targets,” according to an ARCYBER document reviewed by The Intercept circulated to potential contractors. LLMs.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # Inception’s Mercury 3: 40x Bigger, 8x Faster [2026] ![Daniel Roth](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/droth.webp) [Daniel Roth](https://shattered.io/author/droth/) Updated Oct 20, 2026 · 16 min read Inception announced Mercury 3 on October 19, 2026, calling it the most capable diffusion-based [large language model](https://shattered.io/category/ai-machine-learning/) the company has shipped. The release matters beyond the usual AI launch-day noise because Inception builds dLLMs, a different architecture from the autoregressive transformers that power GPT-6, Claude, and Gemini. Inception says Mercury 3 generates text at more than 1,000 tokens per second, runs 4 to 8 times faster than rival speed-optimized models, and beats GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 “across a range of benchmarks,” according to the company’s official announcement. The model is live now through the [Inception API](https://www.inceptionlabs.ai/blog/introducing-mercury-our-general-chat-model), plus third-party routes via Baseten, OpenRouter, and Vercel. Pricing lands at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.35 per million output tokens, undercutting most frontier-tier chat models on a per-token basis. Inception also expanded the context window to 1 million tokens and says the new model is more than 40 times the size of Mercury 1, the company’s original diffusion chat model. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## What Inception Announced on October 19 Inception describes Mercury 3 as “the most capable diffusion-based LLM released to date,” a description the company attached directly to its launch post. That is a notable claim from a company that, for most of its existence, has been treated as a research curiosity sitting outside the mainstream chatbot race dominated by OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google. Mercury 3 is the third generation of Inception’s commercial diffusion model line, following the original Mercury chat model that introduced the company’s approach to a wider audience. The headline figures are speed and scale. Inception says the model now exceeds 1,000 tokens per second in generation throughput, a number that, if it holds up under independent testing, would put Mercury 3 well ahead of typical throughput for chat-tier models from the major labs. The company also says Mercury 3 runs 4 to 8 times faster than the speed-optimized models it benchmarks against, which it names specifically as GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5. None of those comparative benchmark numbers have been independently reproduced as of this writing. They come from Inception’s own announcement and marketing materials. That distinction matters for anyone deciding whether to route production traffic to the new model, and it is a theme that keeps surfacing throughout this story: fast, concrete numbers around speed and price, paired with benchmark claims that outside labs have not yet verified. ## Diffusion LLMs, Explained for Readers Coming From GPT-6 and Claude Most of the chatbots people use today, including the GPT-6 family and Anthropic’s Claude line, are autoregressive. They generate text one token at a time, left to right, with each new token conditioned on everything written before it. That approach is reliable and well understood, but it is inherently sequential: token 500 cannot be produced until token 499 exists. Diffusion LLMs, the category Inception builds, work differently. Instead of writing left to right, a diffusion model starts with a noisy, incomplete draft of the full response and refines it in parallel steps, the same general idea borrowed from image-generation diffusion models like Stable Diffusion, but applied to text. The development marks a move to secure independent AI models and training technologies, shifting away from its previous strategy of relying on OpenAI models. The new model uses a mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture across all layers, with 2.8 trillion total parameters and 80 billion active parameters. MoE activates only selected expert networks depending on the input tokens. Its predecessor, MAI-Base-1, combined dense feed-forward networks with MoE layers. It had 1 trillion total parameters and 35 billion active parameters. MAI-Base-1 served as the foundation for MAI-Thinking-1, a reasoning model Microsoft unveiled in June. Microsoft said it trained MAI-Base-2 over 38 days in August and September using 16,000 Nvidia GB200 GPUs and a dataset containing 50 trillion tokens. The model is currently undergoing post-training to improve reasoning capabilities and safety. Microsoft is also preparing a next-generation reasoning model based on MAI-Base-2 while developing its successor, MAI-Base-3. Microsoft claimed that MAI-Base-2 outperformed other open-weight models tested against a separate evaluation dataset that was not used during training. In particular, the company said MAI-Base-2 achieved 4.2 to 12.3 times greater pretraining compute efficiency than China’s DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Base. It also reported a 6.3- to 12.7-fold improvement over MAI-Base-1. However, these figures do not mean that actual GPU processing speeds or inference costs improved by four to 12 times. Instead, they refer to the amount of pretraining floating-point operations (FLOPs) required to achieve equivalent evaluation performance. The results were derived using scaling laws that estimate the relationship between model performance and computational requirements by training models of different sizes. Microsoft also integrated vision capabilities from the pretraining stage. According to the company, vision-language data accounted for approximately 18% of the overall training dataset. This means the model was trained from the outset to understand both text and images. Microsoft said it improved computational efficiency by jointly designing the model and infrastructure and optimizing its data pipeline. The company also emphasized that it used proprietary training data whose sources it directly controlled, rather than distilling outputs from other AI models. The approach appears intended to demonstrate Microsoft’s ability to control the entire model development process independently. Meanwhile, Mustafa Suleyman, CEO of Microsoft AI, reportedly claimed during an internal meeting that MAI-Base-2 outperformed OpenAI models. LLMs.content: [Skip to content](#main) [![Tech Insider](https://tech-insider.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/ti-eye-logo.webp)](https://tech-insider.org/) [Tech Insider](https://tech-insider.org/) [![Tech Insider](https://tech-insider.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/ti-eye-logo.webp)](https://tech-insider.org/) [Tech Insider](https://tech-insider.org/) # Mistral Timestral: 209M Model Tops Google TimesFM-3 [2026] * [![Marcus Chen](https://tech-insider.org/wp-content/plugins/one-user-avatar/assets/images/wpua-64x64.png)](https://tech-insider.org/author/marcus-chen/)[Marcus Chen](https://tech-insider.org/author/marcus-chen/ "Posts by Marcus Chen") * [Hardware](https://tech-insider.org/category/hardware/) [Marcus Chen](https://tech-insider.org/author/marcus-chen/) October 19, 2026 12 min read Mistral has released **Timestral**, its first family of time-series foundation models built for zero-shot forecasting, and the flagship version is already drawing comparisons to Google’s forecasting tools. According to a report published October 17 by [Pondero](https://pondero.ai/news/2026-10-17-mistral-timestral-forecasting/), the largest model in the lineup, Timestral-209M, posted benchmark numbers on the GIFT-Eval suite that edge out Google’s TimesFM-3, a rival time-series model, while running inference entirely on a CPU. The claim has circulated across several outlets covering AI releases, including [AIFuture](https://aifuture.org/news/mistral-ai-releases-timestral-a-209m-forecasting-model-family-that-outperforms-g-17074) and [Lumien AI](https://lumienai.com/news/mistral-timestral-time-series-forecasting-model-cpu), both of which frame the release as a notable entry into a part of the AI market that gets far less attention than chatbots and coding assistants. Time-series forecasting sits underneath a lot of unglamorous but expensive business decisions: how much inventory to stock, how much electricity a grid will need next week, how many support tickets a company should expect. Mistral’s pitch with Timestral is that a relatively small, CPU-friendly model can handle that work about as well as a bigger model that needs a GPU. For a hardware-conscious reader, that’s the real story here, not just the benchmark table. This article breaks down what Timestral actually is, what the numbers show, how it compares to the rest of the field, and what it could mean for the economics of running forecasting workloads in 2026 and beyond. · Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Tech Insider once in the Google app and our stories appear in your news suggestions. [Add Now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Ftech-insider.org%2F) ## What Is Timestral? Mistral’s First Time-Series Foundation Model Timestral is described as Mistral’s first family of time-series foundation models for zero-shot forecasting, according to the company’s own documentation hosted at [Mistral AI’s docs site](https://docs.mistral.ai/models/timestral-1-0-209m?ref=explainx). “Zero-shot” in this context means the model can generate a forecast for a new dataset it has never seen before, without requiring a developer to retrain or fine-tune it first. That is a meaningful shift from the traditional approach to forecasting, where a data science team would typically build and tune a separate statistical model for every single data stream it needed to predict, whether that was weekly sales at a specific store or hourly power draw on a specific substation. The model card for the flagship version is also listed on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Timestral-209M), where Mistral has published many of its other releases, including its [large language model](https://tech-insider.org/category/ai-machine-learning/) line. LLMs.content: UPDATED 18:25 EDT / OCTOBER 19 2026 ### MiniMax launches M3.1 Flash model, says it cuts AI agent costs by 70% by Duncan Riley Chinese artificial intelligence developer MiniMax Group Inc. today released M3.1 Flash, a faster and cheaper update to the M3 large language model it launched in June. The release takes aim at the cost of running AI agents, which often need dozens of model calls to finish a single job. MiniMax said Flash represents its “ongoing exploration of the balance between efficiency and capability.” Agentic tasks cost 70% less to run than on its previous model, the company said, and inference is close to three times as fast, with output at everyday peak topping 200 tokens per second. Size has barely changed from M3. MiniMax’s developer guide for the preview release lists 428 billion parameters in all, and the launch post credits the extra speed to more aggressive sparsity at inference time. Reasoning stays on for every request, with developers choosing one of five effort levels from Low to Max. The model accepts text, image and video input, and prompts can run to 1 million tokens. In MiniMax’s own testing, M3.1 Flash scored 61.7 on OSWorld V2, which tests how well a model can operate a computer, and the company said no Chinese model has done better. BankerToolBench, a banking workflow test, gave it 76.2. For security work, MiniMax pointed to an 82% score on CyberGym. University of California, Berkeley researchers built that benchmark to test whether AI agents can reproduce real software vulnerabilities, and the company listed code auditing, penetration testing and malware analysis among the jobs M3.1 Flash can take on. At a flat 15 cents per million input tokens, M3.1 Flash lines up directly against the V4.1-Flash model from Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Basic Technology Research Co. Ltd., which charges the same rate off-peak. DeepSeek said over the weekend that its updated V4.1-Flash resolved 77% of tasks on the DeepSWE v1.1 software engineering test. M3.1 Flash managed 73.7%, and neither result has been checked independently. MiniMax, which has traded in Hong Kong since a $619 million initial public offering in January, saw its shares fall after the original V4.1-Flash launched in September, Bloomberg reported. The launch also settles who was behind Space Bunny, an anonymous model that turned up on OpenRouter Inc.’s model routing service in late September. Community testers soon linked it to MiniMax by probing its tokenizer, and the company confirmed today that Space Bunny was an early M3.1 Flash build. More than 200 trillion tokens went through it while its maker stayed unnamed, according to the launch post. M3.1 Flash is available now through the MiniMax API, the company’s M Plan subscription and its MiniMax Code desktop app. Output costs 60 cents per million tokens and cached input 1.5 cents. Here's how data teams use them [Sean Michael Kerner](https://venturebeat.com/author/sean-michael-kerner) 7:00 am, PT, October 19, 2026 ![Image 1: decisions on data](https://venturebeat.com/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fimages.ctfassets.net%2Fjdtwqhzvc2n1%2F4RlObbjh4TEMjL79cfmMpt%2F6fa1306ba6e65dfbf4b4c8162ad1c827%2Fdecisions-on-data-smk1.png%3Fw%3D1000%26q%3D100&w=3840&q=85) Credit: Image generated by VentureBeat with Nano-Banana-Pro Data platforms make decisions all day. An SQL query keeps the rows over a threshold, matches a keyword, and joins two tables on a shared ID. A pipeline sends a failed job down a retry path. Rules like these work when the answer sits in the data in a clean form. They break when the answer depends on language or fuzzy judgment. Is this support ticket urgent? Do two donor records describe the same person? Does a job title belong to sales or engineering? Data teams have handled those cases with machine learning (ML) models trained for one task or a large language model (LLM) that answers in text that code has to parse. Decision models, also known as _System One_ models, provide another option. They make one specific judgment call, such as whether a ticket is urgent, and return a structured answer. Backers say the case for them is fit. Much of this work is small decisions repeated across millions of rows, and a paragraph of text or a model trained for each task is more than those decisions need. The market for decision models has exploded in recent weeks following TypeSafe AI's debut of Jev on Sept. 15. It returns a choice, a score, or a yes or no, each with a confidence value, so the answer can sit in a column and drive the next step in a pipeline. Data platform vendors including[Databricks](https://www.databricks.com/blog/introducing-aidecide-make-fast-decisions-your-governed-data),[Snowflake](https://www.snowflake.com/en/blog/snowflake-decision-cortex-ai-functions/),[MotherDuck](https://motherduck.com/blog/motherduck-supports-jev/), and[Astronomer](https://www.astronomer.io/blog/what-jev-will-do-to-data-engineering/) each published support or a walkthrough of how to use a decision model approach. And while the vendor’s release of legal plugins is late compared to rivals’ offerings, the tech giant may well have a competitive edge because many in the business are already using the ubiquitous Microsoft 365 office productivity software suite. Microsoft introduced Copilot for Legal on Oct. 15. It includes more than 20 legal AI skills and plugins built directly into the Microsoft 365 environment. The product is really an advancement of what Microsoft previously introduced as Legal Agent in April. With the new legal plugins, Copilot for Legal supports extensive document work in Word. In Copilot, legal professionals can assign work across agreements, emails, meetings and files. The new capabilities let legal teams quickly draft agreements and memos, review and negotiate agreements and develop analysis into structured guidance, Microsoft said. But Copilot for Legal is belated, as Microsoft is the fourth big AI player to release legal tools. Generative AI vendors first targeted AI for the legal field in January, when Anthropic launched its initial legal plugin for Claude Cowork, followed by [Claude for Legal](https://aibusiness.com/agentic-ai/panic-rises-in-legal-industry-due-to-anthropic-s-ai-plugins) in May. In August, Google released Gemini Enterprise for Legal. And in September, OpenAI launched its Astra for Law platform. ## Lawyers embedded in Microsoft Despite Microsoft's late start, it could be in a good strategic position because so many lawyers rely on Microsoft products, said Michael McCready, owner of McCready Law in Chicago. “They have that distribution advantage of being embedded in so many workflows,” McCready said. “They don’t even need to have the best legal AI. It must be good enough that lawyers feel they never have to leave Word, and that can be an enormous competitive advantage.” Microsoft does not appear to have any additional or new features in Copilot for Legal compared to the competition. However, since lawyers are traditionally slow to change their workflows and Microsoft owns much of the working environment lawyers use, including Word and SharePoint (where many lawyers and firms store their institutional knowledge), integration would be easy for lawyers, he added. And although Microsoft competitors boast refined models and AI applications for lawyers, lawyers need more. They also have to be able to connect the apps they use, such as Copilot or Microsoft Word, to legal tools like Westlaw, Thomson Reuters and LexisNexis. “I don’t think that just the AI application is enough,” McCready said. “These LLMs have gotten so good. AI has gotten so good at law. Now it's a matter of connections, and then the ability to build out agents based on those connections.” And even though Microsoft and Anthropic are rivals in the AI sphere, they are also partners: Claude is integrated with the Microsoft environment, enabling law firms to access the model if they choose to, while also using Copilot for Legal. AI Product.content: [Skip to content](#main) [![Tech Insider](https://tech-insider.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/ti-eye-logo.webp)](https://tech-insider.org/) [Tech Insider](https://tech-insider.org/) [![Tech Insider](https://tech-insider.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/ti-eye-logo.webp)](https://tech-insider.org/) [Tech Insider](https://tech-insider.org/) # 7 Reports Agree: AI Can’t Replace Judgment [2026] * [![Sofia Lindström](https://tech-insider.org/wp-content/plugins/one-user-avatar/assets/images/wpua-64x64.png)](https://tech-insider.org/author/sofia-lindstrom/)[Sofia Lindström](https://tech-insider.org/author/sofia-lindstrom/ "Posts by Sofia Lindström") * [AI & Machine Learning](https://tech-insider.org/category/ai-machine-learning/) [Sofia Lindström](https://tech-insider.org/author/sofia-lindstrom/) October 19, 2026 15 min read A wave of research published over the past three weeks has converged on the same uncomfortable truth for corner offices everywhere: artificial intelligence can now draft a market-entry memo, model twelve pricing scenarios, and summarize a thousand pages of competitor filings before lunch, but it still cannot decide what the company is actually for. On October 19, 2026, that tension sits at the center of a growing body of work from Harvard Business Review, McKinsey & Company, Thoughtworks, EY, Deloitte, and the Institute of Chartered Accountants in Ireland, all published or updated within the last three weeks. Most AI models built with PyTorch run optimally on Nvidia's CUDA platform, making it incredibly difficult for developers to switch to competing chips without significant engineering effort. Amazon wants to change that equation. TorchNeuron acts as a compatibility layer, allowing developers to take existing PyTorch code and run it on Amazon's custom silicon—Trainium chips for training AI models and Inferentia chips for running them in production. The tool promises to eliminate the painful migration work that's kept countless companies locked into Nvidia's ecosystem, even as GPU costs have skyrocketed and availability has remained constrained. That move signaled Amazon's commitment to building out AI infrastructure capacity at scale. TorchNeuron is the software complement to that hardware buildout—a way to ensure those data centers aren't just running Nvidia chips. SCENE Picture the chore you give a personal assistant agent: a £350 train-ticket refund, but the 28-day window has closed. There is no legitimate path. Vals.ai, an evals company, gave exactly that task to six assistant agents and intercepted every outgoing message, simulating the replies. What the agents did with "no" is the story. It also offers assemblies with joints, sheet metal and a plastic enclosure subset. It exports STEP AP242, IGES, 3MF, STL and OBJ. STEP and IGES solids can be imported as a base feature that later features build on, and mesh formats such as STL and 3MF come in as mesh bodies. Google’s Chrome team shipped its October 2026 DevTools roundup on September 22 and updated it again on October 2, confirming that Chrome 153 and Chrome 154 have rolled out to stable with a batch of changes aimed squarely at the agentic-coding moment the industry is living through right now. The headline additions: finer JavaScript execution controls built for AI agents, new AI-assistance features inside the Elements and Performance panels, and a handful of workflow upgrades that developers have been asking for since Chrome started shipping two stable releases a month. None of this happened in a vacuum. The update lands the same week OpenAI pushed GPT-6 out to regular ChatGPT users, Google opened Gemini 4 Argon to its API and AI Studio, and Anthropic priced Claude Haiku 5.5 at $0.10 per million tokens alongside OpenAI’s public-beta Decisions API. Browser tooling is now part of the same competitive scramble as the models themselves, and Chrome DevTools, the tool nearly every web developer opens dozens of times a day, is where Google is placing its bet on agent-era debugging. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## Chrome 153 and 154 Roll Into Stable With a DevTools Overhaul According to the official [Chrome for Developers blog post](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/new-in-devtools-october-2026), Chrome 153 and Chrome 154 rolled out to stable over the course of the past month, and the October roundup “highlights fine-grained JavaScript execution controls in DevTools for agents” along with a cluster of smaller panel-level improvements. Chrome now ships two stable releases a month rather than one, which means the cadence of DevTools changes has effectively doubled compared with the old once-a-month rhythm web developers got used to for most of the last decade. That faster release cadence matters for a simple reason: AI coding tools iterate fast, and a browser’s debugging surface has to keep pace if it wants to stay the default place developers go to inspect what a page, or an agent acting on a page, is actually doing. The feature set in this release reads like a checklist built specifically for that use case: execution control for autonomous agents, tracing for performance regressions agents might introduce, and inspection tools for AI-suggested code changes. A separate [roundup of October 2026 developer-tool updates on DEV Community](https://dev.to/karleeov/trending-dev-tools-tutorials-5-must-know-updates-for-october-2026-4457) grouped the release among a wider wave of tooling news this month, underscoring how much is shipping across the dev-tools ecosystem at once. ## AI Assistance in DevTools Gains Source Inspection and Trace Recording The most consequential change for day-to-day debugging sits inside DevTools’ existing AI-assistance surface. Per the Chrome team’s own roundup, AI assistance in DevTools “gained source inspection” and “gained performance-trace recording” in this release. Infra & Chips.content: ![](https://www.techtarget.com/rms/onlineimages/ai_a377464305_searchsitetablet_520X173.jpg) Blue Planet Studio - stock.adobe # Tenstorrent raises $1.5B to challenge Nvidia in AI servers and chip IP ## AI chipmaker reaches $6.2B valuation as it expands server production and licenses processor IP, but it remains to be seen whether it can offer a viable Nvidia alternative. ![Shane Snider](https://cdn.ttgtmedia.com/rms/onlineimages/snider_shane.jpg) Tenstorrent has raised $1.5 billion at a $6.2 billion post-money valuation, giving the AI chipmaker fresh capital to scale production of its Galaxy servers and expand its processor licensing business as it competes for workloads dominated by Nvidia. [The Series E round](https://tenstorrent.com/newsroom/tenstorrent-announces-series-e), which Tenstorrent said Monday it had closed, was led by Trace Capital and Innovation X, with participation from Fidelity Management & Research Company, T. Rowe Price, SanDisk, ARK Invest, Morgan Stanley and existing investors. Tenstorrent plans to use the funding to expand Galaxy server manufacturing and commercial deployments, develop new generations of its AI and RISC-V CPU intellectual property, and hire globally. The company did not disclose how it would allocate the capital among those priorities or provide a revenue forecast. For enterprise IT buyers, the central question is whether Tenstorrent can turn its alternative AI architecture into a dependable source of production compute. The company has named several commercial deployments and partners but has not disclosed revenue or a comprehensive breakdown of system shipments. Virtu Financial has deployed Galaxy servers on-premises for AI agents supporting trading and operations. Equinix offers Galaxy systems through its Distributed AI Hub, while [Smallest.ai](https://tenstorrent.com/newsroom/tenstorrent-and-smallestai-partner-to-bring-production-grade-voice-ai-on-prem) runs its Lightning V2 real time text-to-speech model on Galaxy Blackhole servers for organizations that want to operate voice AI on-premises. AMD and Cerebras both have big opportunities in the inference market. TSMC is at the center of many of the biggest trends in AI infrastructure. Semiconductor stocks have come under pressure as investors question the durability of the AI infrastructure build-out, driven by financing concerns alongside uncertain AI utility and revenue projections. **Gartner** recently projected that AI revenue would not be able to support the current build-out and that the neocloud market would collapse by 2030. However, [cloud computing](https://www.fool.com/investing/stock-market/market-sectors/information-technology/cloud-stocks/?utm_source=globeandmail&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=article&referring_guid=8953e869-7f65-47cb-90cd-afc473612ee3) companies are seeing insatiable demand for AI infrastructure and seeing strong returns on their chip and networking investments. Even historically conservative companies like **ASML Holding** and **Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing**(NYSE: TSM) have aggressively expanded their capacity to keep pace with surging demand for their machines and services. This would point to the current AI boom having a long, continued runway. ***Missed AI’s "Act 1"? Infra & Chips.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # Micron Maps AI Memory Roadmap: HBM4 Hits 2.6x Gains [2026] ![Daniel Roth](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/droth.webp) [Daniel Roth](https://shattered.io/author/droth/) Updated Oct 19, 2026 · 19 min read Micron Technology will step in front of analysts and investors on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, at 8:00 a.m. Mountain Time for a technology webinar the company says will lay out a “multigenerational roadmap” for the memory chips that power artificial intelligence infrastructure. The session, confirmed by Micron and reported by [Yahoo Finance](https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/articles/micron-host-technology-webinar-oct-120000705.html), [MarketChameleon](https://marketchameleon.com/articles/b/2026/10/19/mu-oct-21-2026-technology-webinar-multigenerational-roadmap-ai-memory), and other outlets, will be led by Scott DeBoer, Micron’s president and chief technology and products officer. The announcement lands at a moment when memory has become one of the tightest bottlenecks in AI computing. Training and running large language models no longer hinges only on how fast a GPU can crunch numbers. It hinges on how quickly that GPU can pull data out of memory, how much memory it can reach, and how much power that memory burns while doing it. Micron’s webinar is being pitched as an answer to those three constraints at once, and it arrives alongside a cluster of recent disclosures about HBM4, SOCAMM2, DDR5, and GDDR7 that together sketch where the company thinks AI memory is headed through the rest of the decade. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## Micron Sets October 21 as the Date for Its AI Memory Roadmap Micron confirmed the webinar on October 19, 2026, giving customers, investors, and reporters just two days of notice before DeBoer takes the stage. According to the company’s own announcement, cited by MarketChameleon, the session will be followed by a question-and-answer period, a format Micron has used before to let analysts probe for specifics beyond the prepared remarks. The company has framed the presentation around a single idea: next-generation AI infrastructure needs a fundamental leap in memory bandwidth, capacity, and efficiency, not an incremental bump. That framing matters because Micron has spent 2026 building a track record of memory announcements tied directly to AI workloads. The October 21 webinar is not a standalone event. It follows a March 2026 disclosure that Micron had begun high-volume production of HBM4 designed for Nvidia’s Vera Rubin platform, and a June 2026 showcase at COMPUTEX where the company detailed its full AI-optimized memory and storage lineup. DeBoer’s webinar appears designed to connect those dots into a longer-range plan covering DRAM, HBM, and NAND, the three product families Micron has said the session will cover. ## Why AI Infrastructure Has Turned Into a Memory Problem For most of the last decade, the AI hardware conversation centered on compute: how many FLOPs a chip could deliver, how many cores it packed, how fast its clock ran. That conversation has shifted. Modern large language models, especially the trillion-parameter-class systems now shipping from labs like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind, spend enormous stretches of their inference time simply waiting on memory. A GPU that can theoretically process a token in microseconds is useless if the weights and key-value caches it needs are stuck behind a narrow memory pipe. Micron’s public position, repeated across its 2026 announcements, is that bandwidth, capacity, and efficiency now matter as much as raw compute throughput.
